extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/history of science; readers interested in scientific method and Bacon's Novum Organum
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for constructing and evaluating natural philosophy and scientific induction as discussed in Bacon's Novum Organum (with editorial commentary). Emphasis on how experiments/observations should be collected, organised, and used to infer axioms and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of experimental and rational faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy ought to arise from a close and holy union of the experimental (experiential) and the rational faculties (ex harum facultatum (experimentalis scilicet et rationalis) arctiore et sanctiore foedere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mere empiricism (congeries of facts) or mere rational construction; instead merge observed material with intellectual transformation and subjection so that memory and matter become fitted to the intellect. The passage urges hope for better results when both faculties are bound together (a union not yet achieved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural history must serve natural philosophy (subordination of facts to theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural history (collection of observations and experiments) must be constructed to inform the intellect in order to found and constitute natural philosophy, not merely assembled 'for its own sake'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between a casual compilation of species/facts and a natural history tailored to provide material for philosophy; collect facts with the aim of enabling inductive generalisation and theory-building rather than mere description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency in number, variety, accuracy, and pertinency of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural-history material must be sufficient in number, variety, accuracy, and pertinency to inform the intellect and be adequate for induction (the number, variety, accuracy, and pertinency of the observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sparse, vague, or unverified collections. Emphasise large, varied, and well-attested particulars; without adequate quantity and quality the materials are 'infirma' and not competent to inform philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate measurement and recording of experiments (weighing, counting, measuring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and experiments must be properly measured, weighed, counted and otherwise precisely recorded (nil debitis modis exquisitum, nil verificatum, nil numeratum, nil appensum, nil dimensum in naturali historia reperitur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt methods of measurement and counting in observations (see references to Whewell and Jevons). Avoid vague or indefinite observational reports; precise quantification is necessary for reliable induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments designed for discovery of causes (not only for immediate usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek and accumulate experiments whose primary aim is to reveal natural causes and axioms, even if they have no immediate practical use (complura experimenta, quae in se nullius sunt usus, sed ad inventionem causarum et axiomatium tantum faciunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect 'fruit-bearing' experiments ('nos hicifera experimenta') that are constructed to disclose causal relations; these should be distinguished from mechanicians' practical experiments made merely to serve craft or immediate ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanicians' experiments insufficient for theory (avoid reliance on craft-only experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics and artisans perform experiments for their own operative ends and not for the discovery of truth; their reports alone are inadequate to found science (mechanicus... non ad alia quam quae operi suo subserviunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base natural philosophy solely on reports of practical craft experiments or popular rumours; instead incorporate experiments conducted with the explicit aim of causal investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments used for revelation of cause must be reliable and decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments intended to reveal causes should have the virtue that they 'never fail or frustrate' and satisfy the investigatory intention (ilia autem miram habent in se virtutem... quod nunc fallant aut frustrentur).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments so they conclusively delimit possibilities and resolve the question—used not to produce a useful artefact but to demonstrate natural causation; prefer experiments that systematically terminate the question posed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience must be written and made 'literate' (experientia literata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions and discoveries should be committed to writing; nothing is properly proven unless recorded in writing (nulla nisi de scripto inventio probanda est; Experientia literata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain written records of observations and experiments; develop methods (tables, catalogues) to make experience consultable and transferable rather than relying on memory or oral report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise particulars via tables and coordination to avoid intellectual confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because particulars are numerous and dispersed, instruction and coordination by properly arranged 'tables of invention' are necessary to prevent dispersion and distraction (instructio et coordinatio, per tabulas inveniendi idoneas et bene disposita).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare living, well-arranged tables for the subject under investigation and apply a prepared, digested mind to them. Use tabulation to coordinate particulars so the intellect is not disgregated by sheer number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not leap from particulars to the most general axioms — ascend by continuous steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect must not jump from particulars to the remotest and most general axioms; ascent should be by a true scale and by continuous, unbroken degrees from particulars to minor axioms, to middle axioms, and finally to the general (per scal am veram... per gradus continuos... a particularibus ad axiomata minora... ad media... ad generalissima).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a graded ascent: derive 'axiomata media' (the truly solid, verifiable middle laws) from particulars before formulating the most abstract axioms. Prevent intellectual leaps by adding 'ballast' to the mind to restrain flights of fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add ballast to the intellect to restrain imaginative leaps (weights rather than feathers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human intellect requires not wings but ballast (plumbum) to curb every leap and flight; imaginative fertility must be combined with strict regard for evidence (hominum intellectui non plumae addendae, sed plumbum potius et pondera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage imaginative conjecture but pair it with critical standards, verification, and rules to prevent premature generalisation; cultivate evidential restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must be more than simple enumeration — use exclusions and rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction by simple enumeration is childish and precarious; a useful induction must separate nature by proper rejections and exclusions and then, after sufficient negatives, conclude affirmatively (Inductio per enumerationem simplicem res puerilis est... naturam separare debet, per rejectiones et exclusiones debitas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ methods of exclusion (method of eliminations) rather than mere listing; look for contradictory instances to falsify simple enumerative claims and use systematic eliminative tests to detect causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide rules/tests both to exclude false theories and to test the truth of adopted theories
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary not only to have rules to exclude false theories but also tests to satisfy ourselves about the truth of the theory ultimately adopted (non solum requirimus reglas ad excludendas falsas theorias, sed etiam testes ad satisfaciendum de veritate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the difficulty of ensuring all possible explanations have been reviewed; supplement exclusion methods with tests of the adopted hypothesis (verification, predictions). Later writers (Herschel, Whewell, Mill) have refined such rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction to determine and terminate notions/definitions as well as to find axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: The induction under discussion is to be used not only for discovering axioms but also for fixing and terminating notions and definitions (ad notiones terminandas utendum est).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the inductive method for conceptual clarification and precise definition—induction helps both discovery and the terminative fixing of ideas/terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine and prove axioms' scope — verify wider applicability via new particulars and predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When constituting axioms, examine whether the axiom is only fit for the measured range of particulars or whether it is wider; test whether its amplitude is confirmed by designating new particulars (examinatio et probatio... utrum... aptatum sit tantum... an vero sit amplius et latius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the axiom to predict or designate new instances; if a generalisation discovers new particulars it gains confirmation (fidejussio); failure to discover new instances suggests the axiom is vain or untrue. Verification and prediction are key tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect a greater and different kind of experiments and continue experience by new ordered methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger abundance of experiments of other kinds than hitherto used must be sought and introduced, together with a wholly different method, order, and process to continue and advance experience (copia major experimentorum... sed etiam methodus plane alia et ordo et processus continuandae et provehendae Experientiae introducenda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move beyond vague or casual experience ('mera palpatio'); institute a law-like, serial, and continuous programme of experimentation and new modes of experiment to advance sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose and record past errors as grounds for future hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose and propose the very errors of the past: the impediments of past errors are arguments of hope for the future (optimum fuerit illos ipsos errores proponere... quot enim fuerint errorum impedimenta in praeterito, tot sunt spei argumenta in futurum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify, list, and correct historical mistakes so that removing them enables substantial improvement; treating errors explicitly is productive for future progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on rumours and unverified popular reports in natural-history compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars have sometimes taken up rumours and popular 'auras' of experience and given them the weight of legitimate testimony; such administration is like governing by street-talk (homines docti rumores quosdam experientiae... ad philosophiam suam vel constituendam vel confirmandam excep erunt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer verified, weighed, and systematic reports to hearsay; require experiments to be 'debitae modis exquisitum' and checked rather than accepted because they are widespread or fashionable.
